title: Writing practice: Class Pets, Fractions and Rain Jackets
description: Eight short writing tasks: choose a class pet, compare fractions, pick a rain jacket material, explain a community helper, tell about a broken-down bus, write a report on bees, pick a shape, and compare two towns.

stimuli.title: Choice: A class pet
paragraphs: Your class may get one pet. Here are facts about two choices.
Fish: lives in a tank. Needs food once a day. Is very quiet. Cannot be held.
Hamster: lives in a cage. Needs food and water every day. Sleeps during the day and wakes up at night. Can be held gently.

stimuli.title: Math problem: Who ran farther?
paragraphs: Rana ran 3/4 of a kilometer. Jun ran 5/8 of a kilometer.
To compare fractions with different denominators, you can write them with the same denominator.

stimuli.title: Data table: Testing rain jacket materials
stimuli.caption: Students poured 100 mL of water on each material for the same amount of time and measured how much water soaked through.

stimuli.title: Table: Community helpers
stimuli.caption: Some people who help a community and what they do.
rows: Puts out fires and helps in emergencies
Brings letters and packages to homes
Helps people find books and information

stimuli.title: Scenario: The bus broke down
paragraphs: This morning your school bus broke down. Imagine you are the driver, Ms. Park. You need to write a report for the school office. Here is what happened:
Students waited at the bus stop. The bus came, but its engine made a loud noise and stopped. You called the school office. A second bus came and took everyone to school.

stimuli.title: Research notes: Honey bees
stimuli.caption: Notes a student collected about how honey bees live and work.
rows: One queen, thousands of worker bees, and a few male bees called drones
Collect nectar and pollen from flowers, make wax cells, and feed young bees
A bee that finds flowers does a waggle dance to show other bees where they are
Pollen sticks to a bee’s body and moves to the next flower, which helps plants make seeds

stimuli.title: Shape table
stimuli.caption: Facts about four flat shapes.
rows: Rectangle with sides 6 cm and 3 cm
Triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm

stimuli.title: Fact sheet: Two towns
stimuli.caption: Facts about Maplewood and Riverside, two invented towns.

items.stem: Which pet should your class get, the fish or the hamster? Write your opinion and give two reasons from the facts.

checklist: I wrote which pet I choose.
I gave two reasons.
I used facts from the list.
I used the word because or the words one reason.
exemplar: Task completion: states a clear choice and gives two reasons that match the facts.
Organization: opinion first, then reasons, then a closing sentence.
Language: uses because, one reason, another reason.
Clarity: a reader understands the choice.

support.clue: Read each list. Think about which facts matter for a pet in a classroom, such as noise, care, and holding.
support.frame: I think our class should get a ______ because ______. One reason is that ______. Another reason is that ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different choice. “I think our school should have a garden club because it helps students learn. One reason is that students plant seeds and watch them grow. Another reason is that they work together as a team.” Notice the opinion comes first, and each reason has its own sentence.

Write your opinion about the class pet in the same way.

facts: Hamsters are nocturnal, so they are active at night and sleep during much of the day.

items.stem: Explain who ran farther, Rana or Jun. Show how you changed the fractions so you could compare them, and tell how much farther the winner ran.

checklist: I told how I changed one fraction so the denominators match.
I wrote the two fractions with the same denominator.
I told who ran farther and why.
I told how much farther that person ran.
I used math words such as denominator, equivalent, and greater than.
exemplar: Task completion: converts 3/4 to 6/8, compares 6/8 with 5/8, names Rana, and finds the difference of 1/8 kilometer.
Math accuracy: all fractions and the subtraction are correct.
Reasoning: explains why a common denominator allows a fair comparison.
Vocabulary: uses denominator, equivalent fraction, and greater than.
Organization: steps are in order with a clear conclusion.

support.clue: Look at the two denominators. How are they related?
support.frame: First, I noticed that the denominators are ______ and ______. To compare, I changed one fraction so that both fractions have the same denominator, by ______. This gave me ______. Then I compared ______ and ______. Because ______ is greater than ______, ______ ran farther. The difference is ______ kilometer.
support.model:
Mentor example about different fractions. “Which is greater, 2/3 or 5/6? The denominators are 3 and 6. I multiplied the top and bottom of 2/3 by 2 to get 4/6. Then I compared 4/6 and 5/6. Because 5/6 is greater than 4/6, 5/6 is greater. The difference is 1/6.” Notice that the writer changes only one fraction and keeps the same size parts.

Explain the running problem in the same way.

items.stem: Which material is best for a rain jacket? Write a claim and support it with evidence from the table. Explain why you did not choose another material.

checklist: I wrote which material I choose.
I used numbers from the table.
I thought about both water and bending.
I explained why one other material is not as good.
I used because or since.
exemplar: Task completion: chooses plastic sheet and supports it with 0 mL soaked through and bends easily.
Reasoning: explains why aluminum foil is not chosen even though no water soaked through (it does not bend).
Evidence: uses specific values from the table.
Language: connectors such as because, however, and since; compares materials.
Vocabulary: uses material, soaked through, and waterproof.

support.clue: Think about what a rain jacket has to do. Check each column for each material.
support.frame: I claim that ______ is the best material for a rain jacket. The table shows that ______ mL of water soaked through ______. Also, it ______ easily. I did not choose ______ because ______. For these reasons, ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different object. “I claim that rubber is the best material for boots. The table shows that rubber let in 0 mL of water. Also, it bends easily. I did not choose paper because 35 mL of water soaked through it. For these reasons, rubber is the best choice.” Notice that the writer uses numbers and also explains a rejected choice.

Write your claim about the rain jacket in the same way.

facts: A waterproof material does not let water pass through.
In the table, plastic sheet is the only material that lets in 0 mL of water and also bends easily.
The test numbers in the table are invented for this practice.

items.stem: Choose one community helper from the table. Explain how this helper makes life better for people in a community.

checklist: I named one community helper.
I told what the helper does.
I told why this is important to people.
I used the word because.
exemplar: Task completion: names a helper from the table, tells what the helper does, and explains the benefit to people.
Reasoning: includes a reason with because or so.
Vocabulary: uses community and the helper’s name.
Clarity: ideas are in a logical order.

support.clue: Read what each helper does. Think about what would be harder for people if that helper were not there.
support.frame: A ______ helps the community. This helper ______. This is important because ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different helper. “A crossing guard helps the community. This helper stops cars so that children can cross the street. This is important because it keeps children safe.” Notice that the last sentence tells why the work matters.

Write about your helper in the same way.

facts: Firefighters put out fires and help in emergencies.
Mail carriers bring letters and packages to homes.
Librarians help people find books and information.

items.stem: Imagine you are the driver, Ms. Park. Write a short report for the school office about what happened to the bus this morning. Tell the events in order and tell what you did.

checklist: I wrote the events in order.
I used time words such as first, then, and finally.
I told what I did and why.
I used past-tense verbs.
I started with Dear School Office and ended with my name.
exemplar: Task completion: includes the key events (students waiting, engine noise, call to the office, second bus) in order and says what the driver did.
Development: explains the driver’s action and its purpose.
Language: past-tense verbs and time connectors.
Format: greeting and closing suited to a report for an office.
Cohesion: pronouns and linking words connect events.

support.clue: Number the events in the scenario one by one. Decide which events the school office most needs to know.
support.frame: Dear School Office, this morning my bus broke down. First, ______. Then ______. After that, ______. Finally, ______. I ______ so that ______. Sincerely, ______
support.model:
Mentor example about a different event. “Dear Office, I am writing about the fire drill in the library. First, the alarm rang. Then I asked the children to line up. After that, we walked outside to the field. Finally, a teacher counted everyone. I stayed calm so that the children would feel safe. Sincerely, Mr. Lee.” Notice how the writer uses time words and tells what he did and why.

Write your report about the bus in the same way.

items.stem: Write an informational paragraph about how honey bees work together. Begin with a topic sentence, include at least three details from the notes, and end with a concluding sentence.

checklist: I wrote a topic sentence that tells the main idea.
I included at least three details from the notes.
I put the details in a logical order.
I wrote a concluding sentence.
I used my own words instead of copying the notes.
exemplar: Task completion: has a topic sentence, three or more accurate details, and a concluding sentence.
Organization: related details are grouped logically.
Language: paraphrases the notes using noun groups (such as thousands of worker bees) and varied sentence structures.
Vocabulary: uses terms such as colony, nectar, pollen, and waggle dance.
Cohesion: transitions such as in addition and as a result.

support.clue: Read the four questions. What big idea do all the notes share about how the bees help each other and the plants?
support.frame: Honey bees ______ together in a colony. ______. In addition, ______. Another important job is ______. As a result, ______. In conclusion, ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about different animals. “Ants live and work together in a colony. Some ants search for food and bring it back to the nest. In addition, other ants take care of the eggs. Another important job is protecting the nest from danger. As a result, the whole colony stays safe and fed. In conclusion, ants succeed because each one has a job.” Notice the topic sentence, the details, and the ending.

Write about honey bees in the same way.

facts: A honey bee colony has one queen, many worker bees, and some male bees called drones.
Worker honey bees collect nectar and pollen, make wax, and feed young bees.
A honey bee that finds flowers can do a waggle dance that tells other bees where to go.
Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds.

items.stem: Choose one shape that does not belong with the other three. Prove your choice with facts from the table. More than one choice can work.

checklist: I named the shape that does not belong.
I used a fact from the table.
I told how the other shapes are alike.
I used the word because.
exemplar: Task completion: names a shape and justifies it with a table fact (for example, the triangle has 3 sides while the others have 4).
Reasoning: compares the chosen shape with the group using at least one attribute.
Vocabulary: uses sides, corners, and equal.
Note: other defensible choices exist (for example, the rectangle with sides 6 cm and 3 cm because its sides are not all equal) if the evidence supports them.

support.clue: Look at one column at a time. In which column does one shape have a different answer from the others?
support.frame: The ______ does not belong because ______. The other shapes all have ______ sides, but the ______ has ______. The table shows that ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different group. “The pencil does not belong because it is not made of fabric. The other items, the scarf, the hat, and the sock, are all made of fabric. The list shows that the pencil is made of wood.” Notice that the writer names what is the same in the other three.

Choose a shape in the same way.

facts: A square has 4 sides, 4 corners, and 4 equal sides.
A rectangle with sides 6 cm and 3 cm has 4 sides and 4 corners; its sides are not all equal. (A rectangle with four equal sides would be a square.)
A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners; a triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm does not have all equal sides.

items.stem: A family is deciding between two towns. Write a paragraph that compares Maplewood and Riverside. Tell two ways they are alike and one important way they are different.

checklist: I wrote two ways the towns are alike.
I wrote one important way the towns are different.
I used numbers or facts from the table.
I used comparing words such as both, also, and however.
exemplar: Task completion: gives two similarities (for example, both have public schools and a library; both have water nearby) and one difference with data (for example, about 8,000 versus about 25,000 people).
Accuracy: facts match the table.
Organization: likenesses first, then the difference.
Language: uses comparison words and comparative forms such as larger and more.
Vocabulary: population, public schools, market.

support.clue: Read each row across. Which rows tell about the same kind of thing in both towns? Which row shows the biggest difference?
support.frame: Both Maplewood and Riverside ______. They also both ______. However, one important difference is that ______. For example, Maplewood has ______, but Riverside has ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about two different places. “Both the beach and the forest are good places to walk. They also both have many birds. However, one important difference is that the beach is open and sunny, while the forest has shade. For example, the beach has sand, but the forest has trees.” Notice the comparison words.

Compare the two towns in the same way.

facts: Maplewood and Riverside are invented towns, and every fact comes from the table.
Both towns have public schools, at least one library, a market day and water nearby.
